---
title: "Tables"
format: html
---

This script turns the results into the two tables a paper needs, formatted and ready to paste into the manuscript, and also writes every result to a CSV file.

**Publication tables, from code.** With [{gtsummary}](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/) [@sjoberg2021gtsummary], the table in the paper comes straight from the data and the models: counts, percentages, tests and odds ratios are filled in by the code and saved as a Word file. When the data or a definition changes, rerunning the script remakes the table, and no number is copied by hand.

Stata did not work this way when this analysis was done. The do-files were written in Stata 12, which had no built-in command to turn results into a formatted table. Results were read from the log and typed into the manuscript tables, or assembled with user-written commands such as `estout`. Stata added `collect` and a redesigned `table` command in Stata 17 (2021), `etable` in a late-2021 update, and `dtable` for descriptive tables in Stata 18 ([Stata FAQ](https://www.stata.com/support/faqs/reporting/stata-versions-table-commands/)).

::: {.Rcode title="Source code"}
The full R script is available at:

-   [`R/tables.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/tables.R)

This R script file is itself reliant on the following helper files:

-   [`R/setup.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/setup.R)
-   [`R/functions.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/functions.R)

The code sections below are imported directly from that script when this page is rendered. The code has been run only on synthetic data; nothing on this page is a study result.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
#| cache: false
knitr::read_chunk("../R/tables.R")
source("_stata_links.R")
```

## Labels and groups

Each variable gets the label it should have in the paper, once: one list for the baseline characteristics, used by both halves of Table 1, and one for the outcomes. The regimen group becomes a factor so the single tablet is the first column.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-table-data
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("prepare-table-data")
```

## Table 1: patients by starting regimen

`tbl_summary()` makes the usual Table 1: counts and percentages for categories, mean (SD) for age, the number missing for every variable, one column per group and one for everyone (`add_overall()`). `add_p()` adds the tests Final Analysis.do ran: Pearson chi-squared without continuity correction, the default of Stata's `tab ..., chi2`, and an equal-variance t-test, the default of `ttest`.

The weighted half of the table comes from `tbl_svysummary()`, which takes a survey design. The design holds the inverse probability weights, so the percentages are the weighted ones Stata's `tab ... [aw=IPW]` showed. `tbl_merge()` puts the two side by side, so a reader can see the groups differ before weighting and match after it. How weighting does that is explained on [Inverse probability weighting](ipw.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: table-1-baseline
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("table-1-baseline")
```

## Table 2: outcomes and odds ratios

Table 2 is three {gtsummary} tables merged side by side with `tbl_merge()`:

- `tbl_summary()` gives each outcome as n (%) in each group.
- `tbl_uvregression()` with `x = str` fits one logistic regression per outcome, each with the regimen as the only predictor, and shows the odds ratio with its 95% CI and p-value. These are the unadjusted models in [8. Outcomes](08_outcomes.qmd).
- The same function given the survey design instead of the data fits the weighted models: `svyglm()` with the inverse probability weights, Stata's `logistic ... [pw=IPW]`.

`tidy_fun = tidy_wald_z` makes the intervals and p-values Wald intervals from the normal distribution, as Stata reports ([Functions](functions.qmd#statas-confidence-intervals-in-gtsummary-tables)). The unadjusted models show how many patients each used. For a weighted model {gtsummary}'s N would be the sum of the weights, not a count of patients, so it is hidden, and a note under the table says that patients without a weight are left out. For the same reason the weighted half of Table 1 shows the number of patients (`n_unweighted`) in its header.

Category codes from the extracts are replaced by readable names before the tables are made (`B` becomes Black; the viral load group `[1000,10000)` becomes 1,000-9,999), because a table label should never need a key.

```{r}
#| label: table-2-outcomes
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("table-2-outcomes")
```

## Saving the tables

`as_flex_table()` turns each table into a Word table, and `save_as_docx()` saves it: the file opens in Word with the layout, bold labels and column headers already set. `as_gt()` and `gtsave()` save an HTML copy for checking in a browser, and `as_tibble()` a plain CSV copy that the automatic check prints.

No journal theme is set. {gtsummary}'s `theme_gtsummary_journal()` can format a table to a journal's style (for example, `"jama"` or `"lancet"`); which journal to use is a choice for the authors.

```{r}
#| label: save-publication-tables
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("save-publication-tables")
```

## Every result as a CSV file

A named list holds every result, including those that are not in the two tables (the sensitivity analyses, the insurance model, suppression at a regimen switch), and a loop over its names writes each one. Each number on [Published results](published_results.qmd) can then be found in `tables/`.

`tables/` is ignored by Git: tables made from real data would need clearing before release, and tables made from synthetic data mean nothing.

```{r}
#| label: write-tables
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("write-tables")
```
